Functions from Series code¶

Back to Functions

The vocabulary of the previous page is closed: a body built from it can be differentiated and integrated exactly because the library can see every operation. Sometimes the formula already exists as code that takes and returns Series — a model evaluated by a library routine, a function with a loop in it — and rewriting it as Function arithmetic is not worth the trouble. function accepts that too, as an opaque function.

Making one¶

Pass a callable of exactly one Series parameter that returns a Series. The result is a one-variable Function whose evaluation calls your code. It supports the same arithmetic as any Function (adding a constant, scaling, applying sin), but the graph contains a box it cannot look inside.

provenance() says how a function was obtained, and is the quickest way to see what you hold:

Provenance

Meaning

Structural

every operation is in the vocabulary; exact derivatives and integrals exist

Opaque

built from a Series callable; derivatives need an explicit fallback (Chapter 2)

Quadrature

an integral that was evaluated numerically (Chapter 4)

Autodiff

a derivative of an opaque function, obtained by automatic differentiation

 
#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace math = pluss::math;
namespace operators = pluss::operators;
using namespace pluss::tils;

static const char *name(math::Provenance p) {
  switch (p) {
  case math::Provenance::Structural: return "Structural";
  case math::Provenance::Opaque: return "Opaque";
  case math::Provenance::Quadrature: return "Quadrature";
  case math::Provenance::Autodiff: return "Autodiff";
  }
  return "?";
}

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(6));
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0});

  const math::Function structural = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function v) { return v.sin() * v.exp(); });
  const math::Function opaque = math::function({"x"}, [](const pluss::Series &v) { return v.sin().mul(v.exp()); });

  out.writeln("structural values", structural({x}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("opaque values    ", opaque({x}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("provenance: structural", name(structural.provenance()), " opaque", name(opaque.provenance()));

  const math::Function shifted = opaque + 1.0;
  out.writeln("opaque + 1       ", shifted({x}).pull<double>(), name(shifted.provenance()));
  out.writeln("sin(2 * opaque)  ", (opaque * 2.0).sin()({x}).pull<double>());

  const math::Function exact_primitive = operators::antiderivative("x")(math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function v) { return v.pow(3); }));
  const math::Function numeric_primitive = operators::antiderivative("x")(math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function v) { return (-v.pow(2)).exp(); }));
  const math::Function derivative = operators::differential("x", 1, {.fallback = math::Fallback::Autodiff})(opaque);
  out.writeln("primitive of x^3:                          ", name(exact_primitive.provenance()));
  out.writeln("primitive of exp(-x^2):                    ", name(numeric_primitive.provenance()));
  out.writeln("autodiff derivative of the opaque function:", name(derivative.provenance()));
}

Output

structural values [0.790439, 2.287355]
opaque values     [0.790439, 2.287355]
provenance: structural Structural  opaque Opaque
opaque + 1        [1.790439, 3.287355] Opaque
sin(2 * opaque)   [0.999949, -0.990537]
primitive of x^3:                           Structural
primitive of exp(-x^2):                     Quadrature
autodiff derivative of the opaque function: Autodiff

The two functions agree to every printed digit, but provenance() tells them apart. Arithmetic on an opaque function stays opaque: adding 1 or scaling and applying sin all produce a working function that still contains the box. The three lines at the bottom preview what the later chapters build on. The primitive of x³ is computed by an exact rule and stays Structural. The primitive of exp(−x²) has no closed form in the rule set, so it is evaluated by numerical quadrature and is marked Quadrature. The derivative of the opaque function exists only because the fallback was requested, and is marked Autodiff. Whenever you hold a function and are unsure whether its derivative or integral is exact, ask provenance().

What an opaque function cannot do¶

An opaque function is a deliberately narrow tool, and the library says so rather than guess.

  • Exactly one variable. The callable takes one Series, so the function has arity 1. A function of several variables must be written with Function arithmetic.

  • No mixing with a separately built function. Two function(...) calls make independent traces, and Functions from different traces cannot be combined; that includes an opaque function and a structural one. Combine them by writing the structural part inside the Series callable instead.

  • No exact derivative. differential on an opaque function is rejected unless you choose the automatic-differentiation fallback; Chapter 2 shows both.

  • No saving. The callable cannot be written to a file (Saving and loading).

  • Errors from your code. A callable that returns an undefined Series is reported as an error at evaluation.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

#include <sstream>
#include <string>

namespace math = pluss::math;
namespace operators = pluss::operators;
using namespace pluss::tils;

template <class F> static void attempt(OutputEngine &out, const char *label, F &&call) {
  try {
    call();
    out.writeln(label, "-> no error");
  } catch (const pluss::Error &e) {
    const std::string text(e.what());
    out.writeln(label, "->", text.substr(0, text.find('\n')));
  }
}

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  const math::Function opaque = math::function({"x"}, [](const pluss::Series &v) { return v.sin(); });
  const math::Function structural = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function v) { return v; });
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5});

  out.writeln("arity of the opaque function:", opaque.arity());
  attempt(out, "opaque * structural                ", [&] { (void)(opaque * structural); });
  attempt(out, "derivative without a fallback      ", [&] { (void)operators::differential("x")(opaque); });
  attempt(out, "save to a stream                   ", [&] { std::ostringstream o; math::io::save(opaque, o); });
  attempt(out, "callable returning an undefined one", [&] {
    const math::Function bad = math::function({"x"}, [](const pluss::Series &) { return pluss::Series{}; });
    (void)bad({x});
  });
}

Output

arity of the opaque function: 1
opaque * structural                 -> math::Function: expressions from different variable traces cannot be combined directly
derivative without a fallback       -> operators::differential: opaque Function requires explicit DiffOptions{.fallback = math::Fallback::Autodiff}
save to a stream                    -> math::io::save: opaque Function callables are not serializable
callable returning an undefined one -> math::Function: opaque callable returned an undefined Series

Each restriction is an error at the point where the request is made, with a message that says what to do. The fix for the derivative error is quoted in the message itself.

Prefer the Function vocabulary whenever the formula can be written in it. It is exact, it saves, and it composes with every operator; reach for an opaque function only for code you cannot restate.
